content:
Extreme Hot Weather Alert takes effect, automatically issues Yellow warning

The Labour Department today announced a new mechanism that continues to adopt the Observatory's Heat Index, but adds two new conditions on top of the existing warning trigger criteria, lowering the threshold for issuing warnings. The first condition is that when the Observatory issues the Extreme Hot Weather Special Alert, the authorities will automatically issue a Yellow Heat Stress warning, while at the same time lowering the thresholds for Red and Black warnings: previously, to issue a Red warning, the Heat Index had to reach 32 or above at King's Park monitoring station, or at four out of the other nine monitoring stations; under the new mechanism, if the Observatory has already issued the Extreme Hot Weather Special Alert, it only needs to reach 32 at King's Park or at two out of the other nine stations for a Red warning to be issued. Observatory data shows that the "Extreme Hot Weather" Special Alert refers to situations where the temperature has reached or is expected to generally reach an extreme level, namely 35.0 degrees or above, reminding the public that the weather is extremely hot and to pay attention to their physical health conditions.

If multiple districts reach 35 degrees with sufficient data to trigger Yellow, it will directly "escalate" to Red

Another new condition of the new mechanism is that when temperatures across multiple districts in Hong Kong reach 35 degrees or above, in addition to the further lowering of the index thresholds for triggering warnings as mentioned above, the existing heat stress warning will also automatically be raised by one level. Hui Chak-sum gave an example: if multiple districts reach above 35 degrees and there is sufficient data to trigger a Yellow heat stress warning, it will directly "escalate" to a Red warning; when the threshold for triggering a Red warning is met, a Black warning will be issued directly.

The new mechanism takes effect tomorrow (28th). Hui Chak-sum said that although this year's summer break is nearing its end, hot weather may continue, and it is impossible to estimate whether temperatures will rise abnormally again, in which case the new mechanism can be applied. Two former Observatory directors previously wrote articles pointing out that the authorities had misused the Observatory's Heat Index, arguing that it failed to reflect the conditions borne by outdoor workers, and suggested adopting the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature used in many countries. The Labour Department said that after the mechanism is launched, it will continuously review its operation and make ongoing improvements, such as researching whether to incorporate Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and other monitoring data as one of the system's indicators.

Under the new mechanism, the hottest day on 8.9 would have triggered a Red warning

After the Secretary for Labour met the press, he further briefed the media. The department cited an example, saying that on August 9, when temperatures broke records, under the new mechanism, a Red heat stress warning would have been issued. On August 8, temperatures were relatively lower, but wind speed and humidity were unfavourable, and a Black warning might have been issued. Under the new mechanism, there may be four to seven days a year when a Red warning is issued, and one to two days when a Black warning might be issued.

Lam Chiu-ying: Continuing to use the Hong Kong Heat Index is "a defect that needs to be addressed"

Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying, who has repeatedly criticised the current work heat stress warning mechanism, described the new arrangement as "a step forward," believing that incorporating temperature into consideration is a down-to-earth and easily understood indicator for workers, and meets the expectations of frontline workers. However, he described the warning mechanism's continued use of the Hong Kong Heat Index as "a defect that needs to be addressed," saying "there is no reason for us to use an unscientific (mechanism) as the basis and then use other methods to correct it." He hopes that the authorities will formally adopt the internationally used Wet Bulb Globe Temperature before next summer. Lam Chiu-ying also pointed out that the threshold for issuing warnings is only a starting point; the measures to cool down workers are merely guidelines, and workers have reported that they are rarely effectively implemented. He suggested making the measures a legal requirement.

Lee Boon-ying: The new mechanism is a "minor patch"

Another former director, Lee Boon-ying, also reiterated that the research on the Hong Kong Heat Index is not applicable to outdoor workers, and the Labour Department's application of the Hong Kong Heat Index is "scientifically untenable." He described the new mechanism's main addition of considering temperature as a "minor patch" that fails to fully account for factors such as humidity and wind speed, "only addressing the predicament of having no higher-level work heat stress warning when extreme high temperatures occur," emphasising that Wet Bulb Globe Temperature has proven effective in many countries. He said that Hong Kong's hot weather has not yet passed, and the protection afforded to outdoor workers remains insufficient; they can only look out for themselves.

ICRC suggests subsidising Wet Bulb Globe Index equipment at worksites

The Industrial Cases Rights Committee said it was pleased to see the authorities optimising the mechanism, pointing out that the Observatory's Extreme Hot Weather Special Alert has a预警 nature, and incorporating the special alert into consideration would make it easier to trigger higher-level warnings, reflecting the heat stress on outdoor workers. The committee also recommended that the government promote and subsidise companies in setting up Wet Bulb Globe Index monitoring equipment at worksites, so that employers can adjust work arrangements according to on-site conditions.

ICRC also pointed out that if workers' working conditions do not improve after a warning is issued, the warning would be useless. It recommended improving the existing "Guidelines on the Prevention of Heat Stroke at Work," specifying that when a Black heat stress warning is issued, high-risk outdoor work must be suspended; for other levels, workers should be guaranteed the right to take rest as needed, and employers must not impose penalties.

Greenpeace said this adjustment is old wine in a new bottle. Without using Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and continuing to use the "Hong Kong Heat Index" that does not meet actual needs, it cannot reflect the actual heat stress faced by outdoor workers, and the protection is limited. Greenpeace project officer Yang Jie-li said the current update is like scratching the surface. She pointed out that the conditions for issuing Red and Black work heat stress warnings still rely on the Hong Kong Heat Index, which has a relatively low weighting for "heat radiation" and is unsuitable for measuring the heat stress of outdoor workers, lacking scientific basis. She said the Labour Department's continued use of the wrong indicator greatly reduces protection for workers.
